quotes.locator: Section 4.2 "Objections to singularities", subsection "Search Limits"
quotes.passage: A second kind of bottleneck may occur even with complete automation. This type of bottleneck occurs when the creative search process itself prevents especially rapid producitivy gains.

quotes.locator: Abstract
quotes.passage: One theme that emerges is based on Baumol's "cost disease" insight: growth may be constrained not by what we are good at but rather by what is essential and yet hard to improve.

quotes.locator: Section 4.1, Example 3 "Singularities without Complete Automation", first paragraph
quotes.passage: With the CES case and an elasticity of substitution less than one, we require that all tasks are automated. If only a fraction of the tasks are automated, then the scarce factor (labor) will dominate, and growth rates do not explode.

quotes.locator: Section 4.2 "Objections to singularities", subsection "Baumol Tasks and Natural Laws"
quotes.passage: A third kind of bottleneck may occur even with complete automation and even with a superintelligence. This type of bottleneck occurs when an essential input does not see much productivity growth.

title: Explosive growth from AI automation: A review of the arguments

quotes.locator: Section 1 (Introduction), list of four themes, first theme "Growth theory models predict explosive growth"
quotes.passage: Growth theory models often predict explosive growth by default when AI is able to substitute for human labor on most or all tasks in the economy.

quotes.locator: Section 2.3 "AI automation could have massive transitory effects", paragraph beginning "Overall, even if the other arguments"
quotes.passage: there's still room for explosive growth if AI can automate e.g. 90% of tasks in the economy and it can do so in a period of less than 10 years.

quotes.locator: Section 3.1 "Regulations can slow down the economic impact of AI", paragraph beginning "In light of the above discussion"
quotes.passage: we think our baseline scenario here for AI regulation should be more like nuclear arms control and less like the regulation of nuclear energy

quotes.locator: Section 3.2 "Output is bottlenecked by other non-accumulable factors of production", paragraph containing "there might be intrinsic timescales"
quotes.passage: Some version of this argument is certainly sound: there must eventually be some resource constraints that prevent output from growing arbitrarily large. The important question about this argument is not whether it holds eventually, but whether it holds quickly enough to preclude explosive growth.

quotes.locator: Section 1 (Introduction), fourth theme
quotes.passage: We think that the odds of widespread automation and subsequent explosive growth by the end of this century are about even.

title: Could Advanced AI Drive Explosive Economic Growth?

quotes.locator: Section "AI robots as a form of labor"
quotes.passage: In this (extreme!) fiction, AI robots can perfectly substitute for all human labor.

quotes.locator: Summary, first argument ("Idea-based models of very long-run growth imply AI could drive explosive growth")
quotes.passage: Suppose we develop AI systems that can substitute very effectively for human labor in producing output and in R&D. The following ideas feedback loop could occur: more ideas → more output → more AI systems → more ideas…

quotes.locator: Summary, first argument, same paragraph, after the feedback loop
quotes.passage: Before 1880, the ideas feedback loop led to super-exponential growth. So our default expectation should be that this new ideas feedback loop will again lead to super-exponential growth.

quotes.locator: Summary, third argument ("An ignorance perspective assigns some probability to explosive growth")
quotes.passage: But we do know that the pace of growth has increased significantly over the course of history. Absent deeper understanding of the mechanics driving growth, it would be strange to rule out growth increasing again.

quotes.locator: Summary, objection "Automation limits", response
quotes.passage: I don't think this provides a decisive reason to rule out explosive growth. Firstly, it's possible that we will ultimately automate all essential tasks, or restructure work-flows to do without them.

quotes.locator: Summary, objection "Limits to how fast a human economy can grow", response
quotes.passage: I do think that there is some chance that one of these bottlenecks will prevent explosive growth. On the other hand, no individual bottleneck is certain to apply and there are some reasons to think we could grow at 30% per year

quotes.locator: Summary, objection "There's no evidence of explosive growth in any economic sub-sector", response
quotes.passage: The absence of these signs in macroeconomic data is reason to doubt explosive growth will occur within the next couple of decades. Beyond this time frame, it is hard to draw conclusions.

quotes.locator: Abstract
quotes.passage: Ultimately, I find that explosive growth by 2100 is plausible but far from certain.

quotes.locator: Appendix G "How I decide my overall probability of explosive growth by 2100"
quotes.passage: What is robust is that I assign non-negligible probability (>10%) to explosive growth, exponential growth, and sub-exponential growth.
